subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Protect Our Planet
hook: Two friends learn how Earth supports all life and explore ways to protect it for future generations.

slides.title: Earth - Our Shared Home
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya visit an environmental center with Eco Uncle to learn about protecting our planet.

image.alt: Earth - Our Shared Home — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: One Planet, Many Lives
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle begins: 'Earth is our shared home. It sustains 8 billion humans and millions of animal and plant species. Today, we learn how to care for it.'

slides.title: Earth's Structure and Resources
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows a globe with layers: 'Earth has a solid crust, liquid interior, and atmosphere. Each provides resources we need.'

points.text: The crust is Earth's solid outer layer with soil, minerals, and rocks.
Beneath the crust is the mantle and core, generating Earth's heat.
Oceans cover 71% of Earth; land covers 29%.
The atmosphere (air) protects us from harmful sun rays and keeps us warm.
Soil, water, forests, minerals, and fossil fuels are Earth's natural resources.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is layered like an onion, with a crust, mantle, and core, surrounded by an atmosphere that protects all life.

slides.title: Biodiversity - The Web of Life
slides.storyContext: Priya looks at pictures of rainforests, coral reefs, and grasslands. 'So many different creatures! They're all connected,' she says.

points.text: Biodiversity means the variety of all living organisms and ecosystems on Earth.
Over 8 million species of animals, plants, fungi, and microbes exist.
Each species plays a role: plants produce oxygen, pollinators spread seeds, predators control pests.
Ecosystems are communities of organisms and their environment, interdependent.
Rainforests, grasslands, deserts, oceans, and wetlands each have unique biodiversity.
Loss of one species can affect the whole ecosystem.

slides.inSimpleWords: Biodiversity is the incredible variety of life—millions of species—all connected in webs where each plays an important role.

slides.title: Environmental Problems
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows photos of pollution, deforestation, and climate change. 'These problems threaten our home,' he says gravely.

points.label: Air Pollution
points.text: Smoke from factories, vehicles, and burning waste makes air toxic, causing health problems.

points.label: Water Pollution
points.text: Chemicals, plastic waste, and sewage contaminate rivers and oceans, harming aquatic life.

points.label: Soil Pollution
points.text: Pesticides and industrial waste make soil unhealthy, reducing crop yield.

points.label: Deforestation
points.text: Cutting forests for timber and farmland destroys habitats and reduces oxygen production.

points.label: Climate Change
points.text: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂, trapping heat and warming Earth, causing extreme weather.

points.label: Plastic Waste
points.text: Plastic lasts hundreds of years, choking oceans and harming wildlife.

slides.inSimpleWords: Our planet faces serious problems: air, water, and soil pollution; loss of forests; rising temperatures; and mountains of plastic waste.

slides.title: Conservation and Sustainable Living
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle smiles: 'But we can fix these problems! It starts with us making smart choices.'

points.label: Reduce
points.text: Use less. Buy only what you need. Avoid single-use plastics.

points.label: Reuse
points.text: Use things again: old clothes as rags, glass jars as containers, paper bags instead of plastic.

points.label: Recycle
points.text: Separate waste: paper, plastic, metal, glass. Factories turn recycled materials into new products.

points.label: Plant Trees
points.text: Trees clean air, provide shade, and give homes to animals.

points.label: Save Water
points.text: Turn off taps, take short showers, fix leaks, use rainwater harvesting.

points.label: Save Energy
points.text: Use LED bulbs, turn off lights, avoid air conditioning when possible.

slides.inSimpleWords: We can protect Earth by reducing waste, reusing items, recycling, planting trees, and saving water and energy.

slides.title: Renewable Energy - Clean Power
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows solar panels on the roof. 'Energy from the sun, wind, and water are clean and endless.'

points.label: Solar Energy
points.text: Panels convert sunlight into electricity. No pollution, lasts millions of years.

points.label: Wind Energy
points.text: Wind turbines use wind to generate electricity. Common in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.

points.label: Hydroelectric Energy
points.text: Dams use flowing water to produce electricity without burning fossil fuels.

points.label: Biogas
points.text: Farm waste and cow dung are converted to cooking gas, reducing waste.
Renewable energy replaces coal, oil, and natural gas, stopping greenhouse gas emissions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Renewable energy from the sun, wind, and water powers homes without pollution and lasts forever.

image.alt: Renewable Energy - Clean Power — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: Global Cooperation for Earth
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: 'Can one country fix Earth's problems alone?' Eco Uncle shakes his head: 'No, the whole world must work together.'

points.text: The United Nations brings countries together to protect the environment.
Paris Climate Agreement: Nations pledged to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Protected areas and national parks preserve biodiversity.
International laws ban harmful chemicals and regulate whaling and poaching.
NGOs (non-governmental organizations) work globally on environmental issues.
Young activists push governments to act faster on climate change.

slides.inSimpleWords: Countries, organizations, and people worldwide must work together to protect oceans, forests, atmosphere, and wildlife.

image.alt: Global Cooperation for Earth — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: Carbon Footprint Calculation
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle teaches them: 'Every activity releases carbon dioxide. This is your carbon footprint.'

example.problem: Ravi's family activities per day: car drive = 2 kg CO₂, electricity use = 1.5 kg CO₂, food = 1 kg CO₂, waste = 0.5 kg CO₂. What is their daily carbon footprint? Weekly?
example.solution: Daily: 2 + 1.5 + 1 + 0.5 = 5 kg CO₂. Weekly: 5 × 7 = 35 kg CO₂. They can reduce by using public transport, saving electricity, eating less meat, and reducing waste.

slides.title: Design Your Eco-Project
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya are inspired: 'What can we do at home or school to help Earth?'

example.problem: Design a project to reduce waste, save water, or plant trees at your home or school. What will you do? How many people will participate? What is your goal?
example.solution: Example: Start a composting program at school. Collect vegetable waste from the cafeteria, compost it in the garden for 3 months, and use the compost to grow vegetables. Goal: reduce waste by 50% and grow 20 kg of organic vegetables for the school kitchen.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As they leave the environmental center, Ravi and Priya feel empowered and hopeful.

points.text: Earth is our shared home with incredible biodiversity and natural resources.
Environmental problems—pollution, deforestation, climate change—threaten all life.
The 3 R's (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) and conservation actions can protect Earth.
Renewable energy from sun, wind, and water replaces dirty fossil fuels.
Global cooperation is essential: countries, organizations, and individuals must work together.
Young people like Ravi and Priya are the future guardians of Earth.
Small actions by millions of people can create big, positive change.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is our only home, and protecting it is everyone's responsibility. By reducing waste, saving resources, and acting together, we can create a healthy planet for future generations.

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Sweet Cake Adventure
hook: Two friends divide a birthday cake and discover the magic of fractions.

slides.title: The Birthday Cake Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother baked a big round cake. She asked Anaya and Ravi to divide it fairly among their 4 friends. Anaya cut the cake into 4 equal pieces.

points.label: Setup
points.text: One whole cake divided into 4 equal parts

slides.inSimpleWords: One cake cut into 4 equal pieces makes fractions.

image.alt: The Birthday Cake Puzzle — Fractions

slides.title: Understanding Numerator and Denominator
slides.storyContext: Ravi pointed at one slice. 'That's 1 out of 4 pieces,' he said. Anaya wrote: 1/4.

points.label: Numerator
points.text: The number on top (1) = how many pieces we take

points.label: Denominator
points.text: The number below (4) = total equal pieces

points.label: Fraction
points.text: 1/4 means one part out of four

slides.inSimpleWords: Top number = pieces taken. Bottom number = total pieces.

image.alt: Understanding Numerator and Denominator — Fractions

slides.title: Working with Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya took 2 slices for herself and Ravi. That was 2/4 of the cake.

example.problem: If Anaya eats 2 slices out of 4, what fraction is that?
example.solution: 2 slices taken ÷ 4 total slices = 2/4 (which simplifies to 1/2)

points.label: Remember
points.text: Multiple parts of the same fraction add together

slides.inSimpleWords: Two slices out of four is 2/4 or half the cake.

image.alt: Working with Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mother cut another identical cake into 8 pieces. Ravi took 4 slices from this cake. 'Look, Anaya! I have the same amount as you!' he said.

points.label: Same Amount
points.text: 2/4 from first cake = 4/8 from second cake

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Different fractions, same value

slides.inSimpleWords: Half a cake = 2/4 = 4/8. Different numbers, same part.

image.alt: Equivalent Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: At the party, Anaya's friend got 1/2 of a chocolate bar, and another friend got 2/4 of an identical bar. 'They're the same!' said Ravi.

example.solution: 1/2 = 2/4. They are equal; neither is bigger.

points.label: Tip
points.text: Draw or fold paper to see equivalent fractions

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount, just different names.

image.alt: Comparing Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Your Fraction Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya has a ribbon 1 meter long. She cuts it into 5 equal pieces for her hair clips. Ravi asks: 'What fraction is each piece?'

points.label: Think
points.text: If 1 ribbon is cut into 5 equal pieces, each piece is __/5

slides.inSimpleWords: One ribbon, five equal pieces: each piece is 1/5.

image.alt: Your Fraction Challenge — Fractions

slides.title: Fractions in Daily Life
slides.storyContext: Anaya realized fractions are everywhere: half a glass of milk, one-third of the journey completed, two-quarter hours at school.

points.label: Milk
points.text: 1/2 cup of milk

points.label: Time
points.text: 1/3 of the day

points.label: Distance
points.text: 2/4 of the road

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions help us describe parts of things in real life.

image.alt: Fractions in Daily Life — Fractions

slides.title: Adding Simple Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi ate 1/4 of a pizza. Anaya ate 2/4 of the same pizza. Together, how much did they eat?

points.label: Rule
points.text: Same denominator? Add top numbers only.

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/4 plus 2/4 equals 3/4 of the pizza.

image.alt: Adding Simple Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Proper and Improper Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya's bakery sold cakes in pieces. If someone bought 5 pieces when each whole cake had 4 pieces, that's 5/4 (more than one whole cake!).

points.label: Proper Fraction
points.text: Numerator < Denominator (less than 1 whole)

points.label: Improper Fraction
points.text: Numerator ≥ Denominator (more than or equal to 1 whole)

slides.inSimpleWords: 5/4 is bigger than one whole cake piece.

image.alt: Proper and Improper Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Lesson
slides.storyContext: The friends learned that fractions are parts of wholes, written with numerator and denominator, and found everywhere from cakes to ribbons to journeys.

points.label: Numerator
points.text: Number of parts we take (top)

points.label: Denominator
points.text: Total equal parts (bottom)

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Different fractions, same value

points.label: Real Life
points.text: Fractions describe portions of everything

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions name parts of a whole using two numbers.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Lesson — Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Ravi and Anaya's Compass Adventure
hook: Two friends use a spinning compass to discover how turns create angles.

slides.title: The Spinning Compass Game
slides.storyContext: Ravi found a toy compass on the beach. Anaya asked him to spin it slowly. 'When it completes one full turn, that's a complete angle,' she explained, pointing at how the needle went all the way around.

points.label: Complete Turn
points.text: One full spin = 360 degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: One full spin around is called 360 degrees.

image.alt: The Spinning Compass Game — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Understanding Right Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya held the compass steady and told Ravi to spin it just one-quarter of the way. 'Stop!' she said. The needle had turned 90 degrees. 'That's a right angle,' Anaya smiled, 'like the corner of our classroom door.'

points.label: Right Angle
points.text: 90 degrees = one quarter turn

points.label: Symbol
points.text: A small square in the corner marks a right angle

points.label: Examples
points.text: Corners of books, doors, windows

slides.inSimpleWords: 90 degrees is one-quarter turn, like a door corner.

image.alt: Understanding Right Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Measuring Angles with Turns
slides.storyContext: Ravi turned the compass halfway around. Anaya counted: '180 degrees! That's a straight line, Ravi.' They realized half a turn makes a straight angle.

example.problem: If Ravi spins the compass halfway, how many degrees has he turned?

points.label: Straight Angle
points.text: 180 degrees = half turn

slides.inSimpleWords: Halfway around is 180 degrees, making a straight line.

image.alt: Measuring Angles with Turns — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Acute, Right, and Obtuse Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya taught Ravi three types of angles using her arms. A small hug (arms close) = acute angle (less than 90°). Arms at a corner = right angle (90°). A big hug (arms wide) = obtuse angle (more than 90° but less than 180°).

points.label: Acute
points.text: Less than 90 degrees (small angle)

points.label: Right
points.text: Exactly 90 degrees (corner)

points.label: Obtuse
points.text: More than 90 but less than 180 degrees (wide)

slides.inSimpleWords: Three angle types: small, corner, or wide hug.

image.alt: Acute, Right, and Obtuse Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Finding Angles in Your Classroom
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya walked around their school. They found a right angle where the wall meets the floor (90°), an acute angle at the roof peak, and an obtuse angle at the open window.

example.problem: The window opens 120 degrees. Is this acute, right, or obtuse?
example.solution: 120° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it's obtuse.

points.label: Remember
points.text: 90° = right, less = acute, more = obtuse

slides.inSimpleWords: 120 degrees is wider than a corner, so it's obtuse.

image.alt: Finding Angles in Your Classroom — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Protractor: The Angle Measuring Tool
slides.storyContext: Anaya pulled out a protractor. 'This tool measures angles!' she said. She placed it on the compass where the needle pointed and read the number: 45 degrees. Ravi marveled: 'That's exactly one-eighth of a full turn!'

points.label: Protractor
points.text: A semicircle with numbers 0-180

points.label: How to Use
points.text: Center at the angle point, align one ray at 0

slides.inSimpleWords: A protractor measures angles using its numbered semicircle.

image.alt: Protractor: The Angle Measuring Tool — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Estimate the Angle
slides.storyContext: Ravi opened the door slowly and asked Anaya to guess the angle without measuring. The door was open about a quarter way. 'About 90 degrees?' guessed Anaya. Ravi smiled: 'Close! It's actually 85 degrees.'

points.label: Skill
points.text: Estimating helps before you measure

slides.inSimpleWords: Try guessing angles before you measure them.

image.alt: Estimate the Angle — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Clock Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya noticed the school clock. 'The hour hand and minute hand make angles!' She calculated: at 3 o'clock, the hands make a 90-degree angle. At 6 o'clock, they make 180 degrees.

example.problem: At 3:00, what angle do the clock hands make?
example.solution: Hour hand at 3, minute hand at 12 = 90 degrees (right angle)

points.label: Clock Facts
points.text: Each hour = 30 degrees (360° ÷ 12 hours)

slides.inSimpleWords: Clock hands make angles that change every minute.

image.alt: Clock Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Angles in Nature and Design
slides.storyContext: Ravi pointed at the river flowing and Anaya at the trees. 'Branches make angles!' said Ravi. 'So do river bends,' added Anaya. They realized angles were everywhere: bird wings, roofs, ladders, and even the way people sit.

points.label: Nature
points.text: Tree branches, bird wings, petals

points.label: Design
points.text: Roofs, stairs, furniture

points.label: Body
points.text: Arms, legs, joints

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are found in nature, buildings, and our bodies.

image.alt: Angles in Nature and Design — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Discovery
slides.storyContext: The friends learned that angles measure turns, come in different sizes (acute, right, obtuse), and are measured in degrees using a protractor. They're everywhere!

points.label: Full Turn
points.text: 360 degrees

points.label: Half Turn
points.text: 180 degrees (straight)

points.label: Quarter Turn
points.text: 90 degrees (right angle)

points.label: All Around
points.text: Angles in nature, buildings, clocks, and more

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles measure turns and are found everywhere we look.

image.alt: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Discovery — Angles as Turns
